rationale: A wins because it finds a fourth usable protagonist, not just another wrapper: “Wise's stablecoin bet is a public-company signal that regulated crypto rails carry acceptable business risk” turns the listed/profitable fact into a real public-markets lane. B is cleaner on grounding, but “Wise's stablecoin rolls out market by market — a map of where the regulators say yes” stays inside the obvious rails/trend/regulation trio. A has a few overfed phrases, but its proof list and uncomfortable questions would make a founder go get the missing facts instead of blasting mush.
gaps_in_A: “£30B stablecoin bet” overstates the supplied fact. Wise moves £30B per quarter overall; the update does not say £30B will touch stablecoin settlement.
“EU MiCA, U.S. stablecoin bills, UK FCA regime, Asian frameworks” imports regulatory specifics not supplied in the update. Fine as reporting context, sloppy if treated as grounded fact.
“stablecoin legislation moving through national governments” is a shaky news peg unless there is a supplied current legislative hook. Do not smuggle in a peg because the word regulation is present.
“the end of ‘crypto or settlement’” is too clever by half. The real angle is stablecoin as regulated payment plumbing; the phrase fogs it up.
gaps_in_B: It misses the public-company/investor lane even though the update hands it “publicly listed,” “profitable,” and “£30B” on a plate.
“skipping correspondent banks” may be too strong. The set later asks which leg the stablecoin replaces, which means the headline is asserting what the proof section admits it does not know.
“Story type: defensive-comment” is the wrong label for the regulatory-map angle. This is policy/context, not a defensive comment; taxonomy sloppiness matters because it changes who you pitch.
“a map of where the regulators say yes” is only a story if Wise names live and blocked markets. Without that list, it is a promising reporting question, not a pitchable angle.
